criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly characterizes buy as low-fixed-cost, variable, fast-to-ship with strong out-of-the-box quality, and build as high-fixed-cost infra that only amortizes at sustained high volume; the cost, latency, effort, and control claims are all true. Deduct for factual errors such as treating open-weight models as 'free', claiming self-hosting is automatically cheaper or faster, or misstating how the cost structures scale.

Full marks: covers effort/time-to-market, cost structure (variable vs fixed + break-even), quality, and at least one control/compliance factor, AND supplies a concrete switch trigger. Deduct for each major dimension omitted or for giving no reconsideration signal.

Full marks: ties the recommendation explicitly to the scenario's specifics — low, uncertain volume and unproven PMF — and reasons about the volume-dependent crossover rather than asserting a blanket preference. Deduct if the choice is stated without justification or ignores the given context.

Full marks: a well-organized, senior-register answer with a clear decision up front and clean use of the real vocabulary (variable vs fixed cost, break-even, time-to-market, vendor lock-in). Deduct for rambling, contradictory recommendations, or vague hand-waving.

expected_answer_points: Recommends BUY (hosted API) for the low-volume, unproven MVP, and gives a clear recommendation rather than hedging
Argues time-to-market / low engineering effort: a hosted API removes GPU provisioning, scaling, batching, and ops/on-call, so the team ships fast and validates product-market fit before investing
Contrasts cost structures: API is variable pay-per-token that scales with usage (cheap at low volume), while self-hosting is largely fixed cost with GPUs idle at a few hundred requests/day
Notes a cost break-even / crossover: because variable API cost grows with volume and self-hosting is mostly fixed, build becomes cheaper only above some sustained, steady volume
Addresses quality/effort: a managed frontier model gives strong summaries out of the box, whereas a small open-weight model may need eval, prompt tuning, or fine-tuning to match
Identifies non-cost factors that can pull toward build: data residency/privacy/compliance, vendor lock-in, rate limits, model deprecation, or need for a custom fine-tuned model
Recommends keeping the decision reversible — a provider-agnostic abstraction layer and an eval harness — so switching later is cheap
Names a concrete switch trigger, e.g. sustained volume where the amortized self-host cost undercuts the API bill, or a compliance rule barring sending ticket data to a third party
common_pitfalls: Assumes self-hosting is cheap or free because open-weight model licenses cost nothing, ignoring GPU provisioning, idle capacity, and ongoing ops/MLOps cost
Chooses BUILD to 'save money' at low volume without recognizing that variable API cost is tiny at a few hundred requests/day and that build only pays off above a break-even volume
Treats the decision as purely about per-token price and never weighs engineering effort, time-to-market, quality, or the fact that PMF is unproven
Recommends build for 'data privacy' reflexively without noting that hosted providers offer enterprise/no-training data terms, or without checking whether the MVP actually has a compliance requirement
Gives no concrete switch trigger, or an unmeasurable one, so the decision is not revisitable
Hedges with no clear recommendation, or recommends build and buy simultaneously without resolving the trade-off
reference_answer:
For an unproven MVP at a few hundred requests/day, I would BUY: use a hosted LLM API for the summarization feature.

The dimensions that matter here are engineering effort / time-to-market, cost structure, quality, and control. A hosted API needs almost no infrastructure work — no GPU provisioning, autoscaling, batching, or on-call — so we ship in days and validate whether users even want the feature. Its cost is variable (pay-per-token) and scales with usage, which is ideal when volume is low and uncertain: at a few hundred requests/day the bill is tiny, whereas self-hosting means paying for GPUs that mostly sit idle, plus the ongoing ops/MLOps burden. A frontier managed model also gives strong summary quality out of the box, while a small open-weight model may need prompt tuning, evaluation, and possibly fine-tuning to match it.

Build wins later, not now. The two costs cross over: API cost grows roughly linearly with volume, self-hosting is mostly fixed, so above some sustained, steady volume the amortized infra becomes cheaper. Other pulls toward build are hard data-residency/compliance requirements, vendor lock-in, rate limits, or a need for a specialized fine-tuned model.

So: ship on the API behind a thin provider-agnostic interface and an eval harness. I would revisit build when sustained volume makes the monthly API bill clearly exceed amortized GPU + engineering cost, or if a compliance requirement forbids sending ticket data to a third party.
